newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. to keep searching for Hutu refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to keep searching for Hutu refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Aid workers say they will keep searching the jungles of eastern Zaire for nearly 100,000 Rwandan Hutus hiding from rebel forces who international agencies say are trying to exterminate them.

"We will use all means at our disposal to find them. We need more information from the (rebel) alliance," said U.N. refugee agency UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg in Kisangani, the main city of north-east Zaire.

"On Saturday, we will either use new flights or travel down overland. One problem is that the forest is so dense that even on Friday when we saw plumes of smoke from the air we circled over it and could not tell who it was coming from," he added.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, facing a world outcry, told Reuters in the southern city of Lubumbashi on Saturday that he was going to Kisangani, the main city of north-east Zaire, this weekend to tackle the crisis in person.

The U.N. says the rebels, who control the eastern half of Zaire, have chased the unwanted Rwandan Hutus out of camps from which aid agencies and reporters are banned, driving them into the jungle to starve.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan has called it a policy of "slow extermination," and a U.N. food agency spokeswoman, drawing a comparison with Hitler's Germany, said: "The expression 'Final Solution' is not exaggerated."
Kabila has denied that his forces killed Rwandan refugees but said that he would accept independent findings and where necessary take action against his troops.
A U.N. aerial search confirmed on Friday that some 85,000 Rwandan refugees fled into the jungle earlier this week from camps at Kasese and Biaro, 45 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
UNHCR said earlier it had received reports suggesting Biaro had been emptied. A U.N. mission to Kasese, 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani on Thursday found no refugees, alive or dead.

Kasese camp, which last week had 55,000 refugees, had been sealed off for four days from aid workers and journalists. Zairean villagers said hundreds of refugees were killed there on Tuesday and some bodies were buried by a mechanical digger.
The UNHCR spokeswoman said agencies were also blocked from Biaro but an aid worker trapped there on Tuesday reported a train-full of rebels arriving followed by looting and fighting.
The aid worker said the Hutus left Biaro soon afterwards.
The rebels said former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen evacuated Kasese this week and denied slaughtering any of them.

In Geneva, aid agencies expressed outrage at rebel treatment of the refugees, who fled Rwanda in 1994 and are widely regarded there as guilty of that year's mass slaughter of their tribal enemies, the minority Tutsis.

The international medical aid agency Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders) added to the concern by saying on Friday it feared rebels were killing refugees on the road west of the border town of Bukavu towards Shabunda town.

Phil Doherty, an MSF project manager for the Great Lakes region, told Reuters an MSF team to the area between March 26 and April 3 had not seen rebels killing refugees but rebels were on the watch for Hutu former Rwandan troops and militiamen.
"Statements from (rebel) commanders themselves were that if civilians are killed in the hunting process it is unfortunate," said Doherty, adding villagers spoke of killings of refugees by rebels.

"The military told us everyone hiding in the forest is our enemy. They say it is just unfortunate if any civilians with them are killed as well," he said. "We fear that if they (refugees) come out of the forest they are killed by the (rebel) AFDL."
He said MSF stopped its work on the road west of Bukavu as it feared it was used to draw people "to an uncertain fate".
